claim: Cortical flow is vital for cell polarization and migration.
source: Cortical flow is vital for cell polarization, migration (Bray and White, 1988; Callan-Jones et al., 2016; Ruprecht et al., 2015; Maiuri et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2015) as well as for formation of contractile ring during cell division (Turlier et al., 2014; Reymann et al., 2016; Salbreux et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Cortical flow is vital for formation of contractile ring during cell division.
source: Cortical flow is vital for cell polarization, migration (Bray and White, 1988; Callan-Jones et al., 2016; Ruprecht et al., 2015; Maiuri et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2015) as well as for formation of contractile ring during cell division (Turlier et al., 2014; Reymann et al., 2016; Salbreux et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: In C. elegans, cortical flow is driven by a gradient in myosin activity (contractility).
source: In C. elegans, cortical flow is driven by a gradient in myosin activity (contractility) (Mayer et al., 2010), transporting the anterior polarity proteins, PAR-3, PAR-6 and aPKC to the appropriate region of the cortex to trigger polarization (Munro et al., 2004; Goehring et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mayer et al., 2010

claim: Cortical flow transports the anterior polarity proteins, PAR-3, PAR-6 and aPKC to the appropriate region of the cortex to trigger polarization.
source: In C. elegans, cortical flow is driven by a gradient in myosin activity (contractility) (Mayer et al., 2010), transporting the anterior polarity proteins, PAR-3, PAR-6 and aPKC to the appropriate region of the cortex to trigger polarization (Munro et al., 2004; Goehring et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Cortical flow dynamics at large scales can be captured using a hydrodynamic theory by considering the actomyosin cortex as a thin film of an active chiral viscous fluid.
source: Cortical flow dynamics at large scales can be captured using a hydrodynamic theory by considering the actomyosin cortex as a thin film of an active chiral viscous fluid (Mayer et al., 2010; Behrndt et al., 2012; Turlier et al., 2014; Tjhung et al., 2015; Marchetti et al., 2013; Fürthauer et al., 2012; Fürthauer et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to theoretical work

claim: Large-scale on-axis (anterior directed) and chiral rotatory flows can be quantitatively described by considering active stresses and active torques.
source: Accordingly, large-scale on-axis (anterior directed) and chiral rotatory flows can be quantitatively described by considering active stresses and active torques (Mayer et al., 2010; Naganathan et al., 2014).

claim: The hydrodynamic length determines the distance over which flow generation ranges and is vital for long-range advective transport of PAR proteins.
source: In this approach, two effective bulk material properties are critical in describing large-scale flows: (1) a hydrodynamic length, which determines the distance over which flow generation ranges and which is vital for long-range advective transport of PAR proteins (Goehring et al., 2011; Mayer et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: The chirality index quantifies the relative amount by which the cortex is rotated compared to contraction and controls embryonic left-right symmetry breaking.

source: At the molecular scale, cortical flow is driven through actin cortex reorganization facilitated by actin binding proteins (ABPs) and actomyosin regulators as well as through force generation by myosin motor proteins.

claim: Large-scale RNAi screens performed in C. elegans 1-cell embryos have failed to identify many of these ABPs.

claim: The flow has a pulsatile characteristic with a periodic temporal increase and decrease in flow velocity.

source: Importantly, ABPs that regulate actin filament turnover such as F-actin polymerizing proteins (pfn-1, cyk-1, arx-2) and F-actin severing (unc-60, fli-1) and capping (cap-1) proteins have a significant effect on the period of pulsation suggesting that pulsation is regulated by cortex turnover.
